fixes.why: The label quotes “bless me indeed”, but the Berean for 1 Chr 4:10 reads “If only You would bless me”. The word “indeed” is not in the verse, so the label says more than its example.
fixes.fix: Relabel to: “If only You would bless me”; “bless the house of Your servant”; “bless Your people”; “May God be gracious to us and bless us”.

fixes.why: The label quotes “from the same mouth come blessing and cursing”, which is Jas 3:10. That verse is in the noun row “The blessing and the curse”, not in this verb row, which holds Jas 3:9 (“With the tongue we bless our Lord and Father”).
fixes.fix: Drop the second quotation from the label, or quote Jas 3:9 instead: “With the tongue we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse men”. Leave Jas 3:10 in the noun row only.

fixes.row: “Blessed are the poor, those who mourn, the meek, those who hunger, the persecuted”
fixes.why: Matt 5:3 says “the poor in spirit” and Luke 6:20 says “you who are poor”. The label gives only “the poor”, which reads as material poverty and sets it against the goods rows. The note says Matt 5:3 is “poor in spirit”, but the label reads the Beatitude as a material claim the text does not state here. Readers from the Lutheran and Orthodox seats would read it as spiritual poverty; the justice reader would read it as material. The label should not decide between them.
fixes.fix: Relabel to: “Blessed are the poor” (Matt 5:3: “the poor in spirit”; Luke 6:20: “you who are poor”), those who mourn, the meek, those who hunger, the persecuted; “if you suffer”, “the one who endures trial”, “the dead who die in the Lord”.

fixes.row: “Blessed is the one who…”: who fears the LORD, trusts Him, walks in His ways, takes refuge in Him; whose sin is forgiven
fixes.why: Example 1 (Ps 1:1) shows the negative form, “Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked”. The label lists only positive acts (fears, trusts, walks in His ways), so the first example does not show the label as written.
fixes.fix: Add to the label: “or who does not walk with the wicked”. Keep Ps 1:1 as the first example.

fixes.row: “The LORD your God will bless you”: said to Israel in the law, in the land and in the work of their hands
fixes.why: These verses say only “you will be blessed” (city, country, fruit, basket) with no one named as the one who blesses. The God-blessed row moves Ps 112:2, 128:4 and Prov 22:9 to “Every other use” for exactly this reason, so the rule is applied unevenly. The LORD is the speaker of Deut 28:1-14 only by context.
fixes.fix: Move Deut 28:3, 28:4, 28:5 and 28:6 to the verb “Every other use” row with a note that they name no speaker; or keep them here and add to this row’s note that the LORD speaks throughout Deut 28:1-14 and that these four verses name him only by that context. The builder should pick one and say which.

fixes.row: Where the verse names harvest, barns, flocks, meat, rain, land, riches or children with the blessing
fixes.why: The first four examples are Gen 39:5, Lev 25:21, Deut 28:8 and Mal 3:10. Mal 3:10 (“pour out for you blessing without measure”, the tithe verse) is the verse a material-promise reading cites most often, and it stands as the face of the row. The note says there is no word on tithing, but the lead makes the row look like a promise. The other side of the contested point has four lead examples of its own, so this row alone leads with the material promise.
fixes.fix: Change the lead to Gen 49:25, Prov 10:22 and Lev 25:21 (a father’s words, a proverb, the LORD’s word to Israel), and Gen 39:5 as the fourth. Move Mal 3:10 and Deut 28:8 out of the first four; they stay in the row.

fixes.row: God blessed: the living creatures, the man and the woman, the seventh day; “the LORD has blessed him”
fixes.why: Eph 1:3 is in three rows of this hub: this one, “People bless God” (as the doxology) and the noun row “Blessing beside the righteous, life, the Spirit and Christ”. The same verse under three headings reads as three claims, and the note already says it is “also in” another row.
fixes.fix: Remove Eph 1:3 from this row. It stays under “Blessed be the LORD” (the doxology) and in the noun row (the blessing in Christ), and the note of this row should say only that it is in those two.

fixes.row: Blessing beside the righteous, life, the Spirit and Christ
fixes.why: The label quotes “every spiritual blessing in Christ”. The Berean for Eph 1:3 reads “blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms”. The quoted words are not a continuous phrase of the verse.
fixes.fix: Relabel the quotation to: “blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing”.

fixes.why: Jer 17:7 and John 12:13 are in this verb catch-all and also in adjective rows (“Blessed is the one who…” and “Blessed is He who comes…”). The note says they are in the adjective section, yet they still appear here, so a reader finds each verse twice and the counts disagree (15 here).
fixes.fix: Remove both verses from the verb “Every other use” row (15 becomes 13) and drop from its note the sentence about Jer 17:7 and John 12:13 being in the adjective section, leaving them in the adjective rows only.

fixes.why: 1 Cor 10:16 (“the cup of blessing that we bless”) is in the verb row “Jesus blessed” and also here. The note already names the duplicate, so this is a placement error, not a judgement.
fixes.fix: Remove 1 Cor 10:16 from the noun “Every other use” row (8 becomes 7). Keep the cross-reference in its note.

fixes.row: A blessing pronounced or bestowed: Isaac’s, Moses’, the dying man’s; taken by deceit, sought with tears
fixes.why: Four verses here (Gen 27:38, 27:41, Deut 33:1, Gen 49:28) are also in the verb row “A father’s blessing”, which tells the same scenes. The noun and the verb are different Hebrew words, so the verses may stand under both, but two rows telling one scene is what rule 7 asks the panel to flag. The rabbi reads Gen 27 and Deut 33 on their own terms and would see the same scene twice.
fixes.fix: Owner decides: either merge this row into “A father’s blessing” and keep only the noun-only verses (Gen 27:35, 28:4, Exod 32:29, Job 29:13, Heb 12:17) as a short noun row, or keep both and say in each note which verses appear in the other.

worker_points.point: 1. Prosperity: the three set-side-by-side rows (verb row 26; noun row 16; adjective row of the poor 16)
worker_points.why: The side-by-side placement and the note are right and take no side, but the goods row leads with Mal 3:10 and so tilts the contest (fix 6). The Beatitudes row’s label drops “in spirit” (fix 3), which makes it read materially on the other side.

worker_points.point: 2. The promise to Abraham: who the offspring are
worker_points.why: Shown by the verses (Gen 22:18, Acts 3:25-26, Gal 3:8-9, 3:14, Heb 6:14), with the note stating no side. The examples show the label.
Limited to the text that says “bless”, with Matt 26:27 (“gave thanks”) named as another verb. The duplicate of 1 Cor 10:16 is a separate fix (fix 10).
The note names the punctuation question and the page does not choose. The row’s label is generic enough to cover both readings.
Note present; the verse sits in the NT adjective row, and the note says readers differ.
The Hebrew is בָּרַךְ and the note states that readers have taken it as a softened “curse” without deciding. The row label names the Berean’s rendering, which is what the rule asks.
The God rows are filled only where the verse names the LORD, God or the Father. The Eph 1:3 duplicate is a placement error and is fix 7, not a fault in the by-hand rule.

worker_points.point: 8. Hard verses kept (Ps 137:8-9, Mal 3:15, Zech 11:5, Ps 10:3, Luke 23:29, Deut 29:19)
worker_points.why: Kept, each with a note and no verdict. The note on Ps 137 says the text does not call the words the LORD’s, which is the right limit.
Shown with the text’s own words (Gen 27:35 “came deceitfully”). The noun-row merge in fix 11 is a separate question about duplication, not about the deceit.

The father’s-blessing, priestly and Balaam rows are the Torah on its own terms, and the gift sense of בְּרָכָה is shown from Torah and Joshua. The Torah-first order holds: the verb and noun sections lead with Gen 1, Gen 27 and Deut 11:26.

examples_checked: 22 of 25 rows show their label in the examples as built (the built example texts were read; the Berean was checked directly for 1Chr.4.10 and Prov.10.7 only). The three that do not are the request row (label word “indeed”), the Blessing set against cursing row (label quote from Jas 3:10), and the first adjective row (example 1 shows the negative form).
summary: The hub holds its contested points side by side, takes no side and keeps the Torah first, so it can ship once the fixes are made. Most fixes are small: label quotations that do not match their verses, a few verses placed in two rows, and one lead that tilts the prosperity contest.
